entries.title: Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes
entries.summary: Authorities are keeping a close eye on cafes, fearing they could play a role in fostering anti-government sentiment.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes

September 9, 2026

Authorities are keeping a close eye on cafes, fearing they could play a role in fostering anti-government sentiment.

Iranian authorities have launched a clampdown on cafes in the capital, Tehran, in recent months, suspecting them of fostering anti-government sentiment and facilitating protests.  

According to the human rights organization HRANA, at least seven cafes and restaurants were shut down on July 19 alone for allegedly failing to comply with mandatory hijab rules.

Previously, some media outlets, including Javan, a newspaper affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have described cafes as "gathering places for protesters" who, in their view, pose a threat to "national security."

Most recently, the "Vanak Park" cafes in Tehran were sealed, resulting in at least 200 people losing their jobs.

Crackdown on cafes

Authorities believe cafes, because of their widespread presence and popularity, could play a role in organizing mass protests.

The government's fears are rooted in the latest wave of protests in Iran, which began on December 28, 2025, and grew into the country's largest uprising since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Saediniya, a well-known cafe chain with 10 branches in Iran, closed its branches on this day in support of calls for strikes. It was subsequently accused of engaging in "propaganda against the state."

Iran's Supreme Court has now upheld the sentence of Sadegh Saedinia, the owner of the cafe chain, to 12 years and six months in prison, along with the confiscation of his assets.

He was arrested over his support for the protests, and all branches of his cafe chain were confiscated and shut down by judicial order.

Other cafes, including "Lamiz" and "Voria," faced a broadly similar fate. Voria is owned by a prominent Iranian footballer. Both were sealed by judicial order because of their indirect support for calls to protest. Cafe closures have not been confined to periods of protest, however, and the practice continues.

The rise of the cafe culture

Tehran has seen a surge in the number of cafes over the past decade, rising from around 300 in the early 2010s to as many as 4,000 now, according to various estimates.

Some experts attribute the growing number to changes in urban lifestyles in recent years. They see this as more than the expansion of a particular type of business and describe it as a sign of wider social and cultural changes within Iranian society.

"The explosive growth of cafes in society can, to some extent, be seen as a social response to living in a state of chronic crisis," Saba Alaleh, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst whose work focuses on political and social issues, told DW's Persian service.

"In such circumstances, people are not simply looking to consume or be entertained. They are looking for a place to temporarily distance themselves from the pressures of everyday life," she said.

"In this sense, the cafe becomes a third space. It is neither home nor the workplace, but a space between the two where people can briefly step away from their everyday roles and pressures, connect with others, and feel that life is still somewhat manageable and normal."

The cafe trend has become particularly popular among Gen Z, who are bearing the brunt of runaway inflation and steep living costs in Iran.

"The young people who gather in these cafes do not necessarily come from affluent backgrounds," Nasser, a cafe owner in Tehran, told DW. "In many parts of Tehran, young people from the middle class also meet at cafes, and many of our customers belong to this group."

The political role of cafes

Even before the latest bout of nationwide protests that began at the end of last year, shutting down cafes was common practice for the Iranian government.

Most of these crackdowns and closures, however, were carried out under the pretext of enforcing compulsory hijab.

The protests that began in late December 2025 changed that, with cafes becoming the target more often and for varied reasons.

"They shut down our cafe on the pretext that we had served customers who were not wearing the hijab, but that is only an excuse," Nasser said.

"Outside, on the streets of Tehran, women and girls have effectively abandoned the compulsory hijab, yet the government expects us not to allow them into the cafe," he added.

Maintaining control over social spaces

Alaleh said the issue is no longer simply about cracking down on women for not wearing the hijab.

"Authoritarian governments generally seek to control the flow of information, social interactions and the organization of citizens," she pointed out. "Any space beyond the direct supervision of those in power that allows trust, dialogue and social ties to develop can weaken part of the government's monopoly over the social sphere."

The expert said the crackdown on cafes and cafegoers is part of the government's efforts to preserve its monopoly over social spaces.

She underlined that to a security apparatus, even a group of young people casually sitting together can represent the emergence of an independent social network outside the formal structures of power.

"The broader and more deeply rooted these independent networks become, the more difficult it is for the government to maintain exclusive control over the public sphere," added Alaleh.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Ethiopia's constitutional reform: What does it mean — especially for Abiy?
entries.summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed stands to benefit from a planned constitutional reform in the country. A new presidential system would reshape political power — and could give him a more powerful mandate in office.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

Ethiopia: What does constitutional reform mean — for Abiy?

September 9, 2026

Does Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed stand to benefit from a planned constitutional reform in the country? A new presidential system would reshape political power — and could give him even more power in office.

Since 2018, Abiy Ahmedhas been the most powerful man in Ethiopian politics, governing the country during some of its most trying days in recent history. From the Tigray war to a feeble but lasting peace with neighboring Eritrea, Abiy has actively shaped and reshaped Ethiopia's role in Africa and indeed the world.

Soon, he might even get to consolidate more power and influence in his office, as Ethiopia's political system might fundamentally change in the future.

Following weeks-long consultations, there are indications that the offices of prime minister and president could potentially be merged. This would mean that the largely ceremonial presidency could thus become the center of political power in the country.

While details about the precise re-designing of the system remain unclear, local reports say that the consultations indeed resulted in a positive recommendation to create a stronger presidency.

For Abiy, that would likely be a remarkable prospect.

Support for a new office

During a drawn-out national dialogue with around 4,000 delegates in Addis Ababa in recent weeks, participants discussed some of the country's key political conflict, including: the overall structure of the state, ongoing ethnic tensions, the rule of law and human rights — as well as the role of the prime minister.

Abiy did not take part in these meetings but could benefit significantly from their endorsement of a presidential system.

One key element for any constitutional reform to be pushed through parliament is already in place: Abiy won June's parliamentary elections with a massive majority, which could help him and his party with advocating for a presidency with broader executive powers. 

Benefits of a stronger presidency

Supporters of a stronger presidency see it as a way of bringing Ethiopia's ethnically and regionally fragmented society closer together.

A president representing the country as a whole could help strengthen a national political identity.

Befeqadu Hailu, an Ethiopian civil rights activist and political commentator, told DW that this might be a strength of the proposed new system, and that a president directly elected by the public would have a stronger mandate to govern.

Hailu believes that in future elections, a presidential candidate would have to convince "more than one ethnic group and more than one religious group" to win an election, which could help strengthen democratic processes.

At the same time, he issued a warning that "[p]residential systems are more prone descending into dictatorship."

How much more power is there to take?

But the key question is not who would become presiden but rather what powers this office would have — as well as who would be tasked with holding the president to account.

Ethiopia already has a powerful executive branch and since taking office in 2018, Abiy has consolidated more and more political power.

The creation of the Prosperity Party in 2019 under his leadership out of a number of coalition partners has already considerably reshaped the country's political system, significantly limiting the role of the opposition.

Abiy already controls the military and security apparatus, with little less power left to grab under a new system.

For British journalist and Ethiopia expert Martin Plaut, the proposed reform is therefore less of a transfer of power to one person that an act of "formalizing the situation that currently exists."

'Legal does not mean legitimate'

The proposed reform also raises a fundamental question about democratic processes: Can such a concentration of power be viewed as the will of the people if it is enacted through legal procedures in parliament? Or should there perhaps be a plebiscite on the proposed changes?

In this context, civil rights activist Hailu highlights the importance of distinguishing between procedural and popular legitimacy. In Ethiopia, he says, existing political institutions have "procedural legitimacy" to enact such changes while they lack broad "popular legitimacy."

Hailu says bluntly that "no one believes that Ethiopia has ever had democratic elections," referring to the most recent parliamentary election, which took place under difficult conditions:

Voting was not possible in several conflict-ridden regions of the country, while opposition parties reported instances of restrictions and repression.

It is therefore unclear to what extent the result of the poll can be regarded as democratically legitimate — yet it is seen as the official result.

This is why Hailu believes that parliament may have the formal authority to amend the constitution and introduce a presidential system while still being only partially representative of the voting populace.

Who was actually included in the process?

Another issue is not only what was recommended by those participating in the national dialogue but also who exactly took part in it — and who didn't.

The composition of the dialogue, which eventually issued the recommendation to change the current system, is a major concern, as opposition parties boycotted the process, while influencial armed groups with strong political aspirations were equally not represented.

Despite certain valid reservations about some of these movements, the result was that some of the major political forces most directly involved in Ethiopia's current conflicts therefore were absent.

Plaut says this leaves only one conclusion: "Without the opposition parties and armed factions, the process lacks the backing of groups that feel alienated by the current system, he explains

"I'm sure that the Prime Minister will get what he wants," Plaut says, describing the dialogue as merely a "rubber-stamping exercise."

Hailu also shared some critical views on the lack of political inclusion of opposing groups, arguing that it was ultimately aimed at implementing changes "based on the vision of the Prosperity Party itself."

No resolution in sight for Ethiopia's neverending conflicts

Ethiopia's biggest challenges meanwhile are unlikely to be solved with a different style of leadership.

Armed conflicts continue in Oromia and Amhara; the 2020-2022 war in Tigray left deep political and social divisions, with many political and territorial issues remaining unresolved despite promising peace initiatives. And nearly half the population continue to live below the poverty line.

Plaut thinks that a new system of government will hardly address these problems; he believes that the proposed reforms amount to little more than "sticking a plaster on what is a gaping wound."

The relationship between centralized power in Addis Ababa and Ethiopia's more than 80 ethnic groups remains unresolved, he argues. Previous attempts to ease tensions between the center and the periphery have failed.

In Plaut's view, the underlying tensions between the central government and Ethiopia's various ethnic and regional groups have to be resolved first.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Oil prices rise as Middle East conflict escalates
entries.summary: The price of oil returned to triple digits in US dollars, as conflict in the Middle East threatens supply chains and puts a strain on global reserves.
entries.content:
September 9, 2026

The price of oil returned to triple digits in US dollars, as conflict in the Middle East threatens supply chains and puts a strain on global reserves.

Oil crude prices topped $100 ($86) a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July amid concerns over oil supplies due to the conflict in the Middle East. 

"The move towards and back above $100 Brent is reflecting a market that increasingly must change its view on how long the Middle East crisis will continue to curb supply from the region," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at the Danish Saxo Bank.

The attacks on Saudi energy facilities by the Iranian-backed Houthisthreaten oil shipments on the Red Sea. This has been a key alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz path. 

Meanwhile, the US attacked Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and in the Strait of Hormuz. "Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies," CENTCOM said in a statement.

Runing out of stock

Since the conflict in the Middle East started, oil exports have been reduced significantly, making some countries turn to their reserves. 

The US has reported its lowest oil reserve since 1982, holding 289.7 million barrels. Former US President Joe Biden and President Donald Trump have used the reserve to cushion consumer prices amid the crisis.

The new price of the barrel is still below the peak reached early this year. In April, Brent jumped to $126 a barrel. Experts believe this is a big risk to a market with little room for capacity to absorb new disruptions occasioned by the war.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Syria arms depot explosion kills at least 14
entries.summary: The explosion struck near the Syrian city of Sarmada in Idlib province in the northwest. The Defense Ministry said the weapons and remnants from the war were being stored temporarily at the site before being relocated.
entries.content:
Syria

Syria arms depot explosion kills at least 14

September 9, 2026

The explosion struck near the Syrian city of Sarmada in Idlib province in the northwest. The Defense Ministry said the weapons and remnants from the war were being stored temporarily at the site before being relocated.

Syrian authorities reported that at least 14 people were killed and another 11 wounded on Wednesday as a result of an explosion at a temporary site used to store weapons and remnants of the country's long-running civil war. 

The explosion took place near the city of Sarmada in the northwestern Idlib province.

What do we know about the explosion?

Syria's Defense Ministry said the weapons and war remnants were being stored termporarily at the site before being transported elsewhere. It said that some of its personnel were among those wounded.

The explosion in an area full of volatile materials led to secondary explosions and fires that hampered the emergency response. Smoke billowed from the blast site for some time on Wednesday.

"The toll from the explosion in a temporary storage for collecting weapons and war remnants near the city of Sarmada ... registered 14 killed and 11 injured in a preliminary count," the Idlib health department said.

Authorities have not yet said what caused the explosion.

It was the second fatal incident of its kind in Idlib province this month. On September 1, five people were killed and others were wounded when a vehicle carrying ammunition exploded in Binnish.

Syria only recently emerged from more than a decade of civil war, when forces loyal to new President Ahmed al-Sharaa ousted Bashar Assad and took control of Damascus. Idlib was one of the hardest-hit regions in the country during the war.

entries.title: How Belarusians still find hope in a silenced country
entries.summary: The documentary "Letters From the Silenced Country" depicts the ongoing repression under the authoritarian regime. Director Andrei Kutsila talked to DW ahead of the film's Venice premiere.
entries.content:
Belarus

How Belarusians still find hope in a silenced country

September 9, 2026

The documentary "Letters From the Silenced Country" depicts the ongoing repression under the authoritarian regime. Director Andrei Kutsila talked to DW ahead of the film's Venice premiere.

When Belarusians took to the streets in 2020 to protest against the disputed results of the presidential election, hopes were high that the regime of autocratic ruler Alexander Lukashenko would end, and that Belarusian society would find freedom.

But authorities responded with an unprecedented campaign of repression that continues to this day. All forms of dissent have essentially been silenced.

It's in this context that filmmaker Andrei Kutsila directed a new documentary that depicts the state's system of repression.

His film, "Letters from the Silenced Country," was co-produced by DW and premieres at the Venice Film Festival on September 9.

A silenced country

Like the 300,000 to 500,000 Belarusians who now live in exile, Kutsila realized that he had to leave his home country amid the state's crackdown on free speech.

While he was completing his previous film — the award-winning "When Flowers Are Not Silent" (2021), on the state's brutal suppression of demonstrations — different colleagues around him were arrested, he says.

Many of them have since been released, "but at the same time, new prisoners are found to keep filling the cells. The situation is not changing; it's even worse now," Kutsila tells DW.

As the film points out in a postscript card, the human rights organization Viasna has documented at least 65,000 politically motivated arrests and detentions in Belarus since the 2020 protests.

"From the outside, people live their normal lives, but the streets have become quiet and conversations are reduced to whispers," says Kutsila. Those who remained in the country can get arrested and sent to prison simply for posting Belarusian symbols of freedom and resistance online, notes the filmmaker.

That was one of the reasons that motivated him to make "Letters from the Silenced Country."

Returning to Belarus and to physically meet and film protagonists in his home country was not an option, so he searched for an alternative way to portray their situation after the protests.

Letters to prisoners served as a starting point to Kutsila's film project: "I read thousands of them," he says.

He then picked stories of individuals — political prisoners, exiles and underground activists — who embodied different aspects of the situation.

Vitold Ashurak died in prison

Belarusian opposition activist and environmental campaigner Vitold Ashurak is one of the film's protagonists.

Sentenced to five years in prison for participating in the protests, Ashurak's fate is portrayed through his correspondence with friends and family during his imprisonment.

Letters from a friend include meticulously selected photographs. Ashurak finds brief moments of mental freedom in these pictures, while the same images are also poetically embedded in the film.

But CCTV footage showing prison guards beating inmates brings viewers back to the brutal reality: Vitold Ashurak died under suspicious circumstances while in custody. His name is remembered as a symbol of the state's repression.

Between resignation and hope

The film also includes animated sequences, based on drawings created by the young student Kasia Budzko, who was sentenced to 2 1/2 years in prison for participating in protests.

Another protagonist in the film is Andrei Ostapovich, a former criminal investigator. In August 2020, he left his position, writing a letter of resignation in which he denounced the police officers' brutality against protesters.

As one of the first security officials who publicly and categorically opposed the Belarusian regime, Ostapovich fled the country — facing many perilous detours.

In one scene of "Letters from the Silenced Country," Ostapovich is asked if, after everything he's been through and witnessed, he still believes in a free Belarus. After much hesitation, his only response is a sigh of resignation.

Filmmaker Andrei Kutsila shares this ambivalence: "Of course, it's in a way my perspective too, as I tried to express my feelings through my protagonists." But, Kutsila focuses on long-term progress, as he adds, "history is the foundation on which we can build a free country."

"You know, 200 years ago Belarus didn't even exist on a map," he points out. There have been struggles to free the country ever since: "So from this long-term perspective, there is a lot of hope."

"No matter how awful the situation is, the only thing that can empower and give us hope is solidarity, connection between people and love. So these are the things giving us hope," notes Kutsila. "And the film, I think, shows this."

Edited by: Brenda Haas

entries.title: Why we're still looking for dark matter
entries.summary: When physicists said they may have spotted evidence of dark matter almost 100 years after it was proposed as a theory, the internet lit up. Here's why we're searching for the thing that holds everything else together.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Why we're still looking for dark matter

September 9, 2026

When physicists said they may have spotted evidence of dark matter almost 100 years after it was proposed as a theory, the internet lit up. Here's why we're searching for the thing that holds everything else together.

On September 1, 2026, scientists at a dark matter detector called LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) reported they had observed an event, a particle interaction, that they were unable to explain.

The team, based in South Dakota in the US, said the event resembled what they think a dark matter particle should produce when it collides with liquid xenon, one of a range of materials used for detecting dark matter.

They stopped short of calling it the discovery, or proof of dark matter, that many in the field have been hunting for almost 100 years.

The term "dark matter" was coined by physicist Fritz Zwicky in 1933 as a means to describe unseen matter that would explain fast-moving galaxies.

The LUX-ZEPLIN observation came just days after the release of the second season of Dark Matter, a sci-fi thriller starring Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly. Both events pushed the term "dark matter" back into people's minds.

Here's what you need to know, with the science separated from the series.

What is dark matter in simple terms?

Dark matter is often described as an "invisible" substance. But it may be better described as "transparent" because it can be seen, or detected, by the gravitational attraction it exerts.

That said, it neither emits nor reflects light, and has never been observed directly. So, in that sense, it is invisible.

Is it true that 95% of the universe is invisible?

Yes, roughly.

Ordinary matter — everything that can be seen or touched — accounts for about 5% of the universe.

Dark matter accounts for about 27%, and dark energy, a separate force linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe, about 68%. Together they account for about 95%.

A different figure of 85% is dark matter's share of matter alone.

But does dark matter really exist?

The strongest evidence that dark matter exists comes from the so-called Bullet Cluster, which formed when two galaxy clusters collided. The collision produced hot gas clouds that interacted. This interaction showed revealed mass in the gas clouds that distributed differently from the gas. Researchers said that mass could be dark matter.

How do scientists search for dark matter on Earth?

Scientists use detectors like the LUX-ZEPLIN that passively wait for interactions between naturally occurring particles and detect radiation.

They tend to be buried deep underground, where the surrounding rock blocks cosmic radiation that would otherwise distort signals.

They are built from materials chosen for their very low levels of trace radioactivity, so a genuine detection is not lost in background noise.

The LUX-ZEPLIN detector specifically works by watching for a faint flash of light and pulse of electric charge released when a passing particle strikes a liquid xenon particle. Liquid xenon, a noble gas, has good properties for detecting radiation.

What is dark matter made of?

The leading candidate particles are:

WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles, are the longest-standing theory. They are heavy and interact only rarely with ordinary matter.

Axions, which are lighter and behave more coherently than WIMPs. A team at Kyoto University, Japan, say data from Earth's magnetic field could be used to search for axions.

What does dark matter do to humans?

Dark matter passes through the body constantly, without measurable effect. Billions of candidate particles cross through a person every second, but only about ten strike a nucleus in the body over a year.

The resulting radiation exposure is far lower than what people receive from radon or cosmic rays.

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

entries.title: Cambodia's floating schools hit by rising fuel costs
entries.summary: The Iran war has sent fuel prices higher in Cambodia, squeezing families who rely on fishing and boats for their livelihoods. For children living on Tonle Sap, rising fuel costs pose yet another barrier to education.
entries.content:
September 9, 2026

The Iran war has sent fuel prices higher in Cambodia, squeezing families who rely on fishing and boats for their livelihoods. For children living on Tonle Sap, rising fuel costs pose yet another barrier to education.

Every morning, 12-year-old Soksan Set faces a journey most children his age never have to think about. Outside his home, there is no road, only water.

Soksan lives in Prek Toal, a floating community on Tonle Sap, Southeast Asia's largest freshwater lake where boats are the main means of transport. A Grade 4 student at the local primary school, he travels several kilometers on water to attend class and sometimes helps younger children along the way. 

But increasingly, the biggest obstacle between Soksan and his classroom is not distance. It is fuel. His family, like many others in the commune, depends on fishing for their livelihood. When fuel prices rise, they are forced to make difficult choices.

"When gasoline prices go up, we don't have enough money to take our children to school regularly," said Soksan's father, 41-year-old Set Soeum. "We don't catch enough fish, and we need around three liters (0.8 gallons) of gasoline a day to travel long distances for fishing. Because of this, Soksan often has to miss school."

For families living on the water, rising fuel costs can quickly become a barrier to education. 

Why rising fuel costs hit Cambodia's poor the hardest

Cambodia relies heavily on imported fuel, leaving households exposed to global price shocks and regional supply disruptions. The 2026 Iran war has driven up energy costs, making transport to remote communities more expensive. Around Tonle Sap, this has hit students and their families. 

Gasoline prices rose 45% and diesel prices more than 70% in March, the largest single-month increase since 2008, according to the World Bank.

Gasoline currently costs 5,700 riel ($1.41, €1.21) per liter, up 26.7% from 4,500 riel a year ago, according to Global Petrol Prices.

Although Cambodia does not depend directly on the Strait of Hormuz for most of its fuel imports, it is exposed to higher global oil prices and supply disruptions affecting regional suppliers. Cambodia imports all of its petroleum products and has no domestic refining capacity. 

For Soksan's family, the pressure is felt both on the fishing boat and the school boat. Some days, they borrow money to buy gasoline. On other days, they cut back on food, clothing or school supplies.

"Five students collect money to buy gasoline, sometimes just one liter at a time," Soksan said. When they cannot afford even that, they row themselves. "We row the boat ourselves. It can take up to an hour, but we still try to go to school," he noted.

On the Tonle Sap, 12-year-old Siyien Ly walks more than 30 minutes to school during the dry season. When flooding makes the roads impassable, she relies on an aid-supported school boat. Some of her classmates have stopped attending, because their families cannot afford the cost of transport.

"Even though fuel prices are rising, we still keep trying to come to school because education is important for our future," Siyien said.

Siyien's family of six has four children in school. Her mother, Kunthea Chin, now sells sugarcane juice after Siyien's father developed serious hearing problems following a water-related accident.

Kunthea said that her daily income has fallen by around half from about $20 to around $10 while the cost of supplies has risen. The family spends around $150 a month on fuel, which they need for both the children's transport and her business.

Taking risks to reach the classroom

Families also try to reduce costs by traveling together and sharing fuel expenses. Some have returned to traditional rowing boats. But saving money can come at the cost of safety.

When several children share a small boat, it can become crowded. During storms and heavy rain, parents worry about their children's safety on the water.

"My mother worries when too many students ride together," Siyien said.

Remote schools also depend on boats to transport teachers, textbooks, classroom materials, food and maintenance supplies. Higher fuel prices can therefore increase the cost of delivering education itself.

"For children living in floating and remote communities, access to education depends not only on having a school, but also on being able to reach it," said Samphors Vorn, country director of Action Education in Cambodia.

"When fuel prices rise, the cost of that journey rises with them. For families already living with very limited incomes, this can turn transportation into a barrier to attendance and, ultimately, to a child's right to education."

The Cambodian government has introduced measures to cushion consumers from international fuel-price increases, including fuel discounts, tax reductions and zero customs duties on fuel imports.

But subsidies at the pump cannot fully shield families whose incomes remain low and unpredictable.

Climate and economic shocks deepen education woes

In 2025, DW reported from the region on how climate change was disrupting children's education. Rising and falling water levels, extreme weather and the dangers of traveling by boat were making it harder for children in floating communities to reach school.

The challenges have since deepened.

Today, 14-year-old Nary is no longer in the classroom. She has been unable to return because of persistent headaches following health complications linked to suspected long-term meningitis.

Her younger sister, 11-year-old Naren, continues to attend Grade 2. She relies on a school boat and pays around 12 cents for the return journey.

For their family, even small costs matter. Their father, Tit Sarin, earns around $7.50 a day from traditional fishing. But traveling farther across the lake to find fish can require about six liters of fuel, costing roughly $6.60.

"When we cannot afford fuel, we have to find other work," he said.

The family then works as day laborers, picking chilies for as little as 25 cents per kilogram. For families like Nary's, climate change and rising fuel costs are now a double burden.

Nary hopes to return to learning. Her father is saving to buy a boat dedicated to shuttling his children to school and back home.

This report was made possible by inputs from Education Above All foundation.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: EU proposes more restrictions for Airbnb, holiday rentals
entries.summary: The European Union wants tighter rules on short-term rentals to tackle housing shortages in tourist hotspots.
entries.content:
Europe

EU proposes more restrictions for Airbnb, holiday rentals

September 9, 2026

The European Union wants tighter rules on short-term rentals to tackle housing shortages in tourist hotspots.

Airbnb and other companies providing short-term home rentals could face tighter restrictions after the European Commission proposed new rules on Wednesday to help tackle housing shortages in tourist hotspots.

A surge in short-term holiday rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing and a spike in housing prices in many of Europe's most popular tourist destinations, prompting residents to protest in recent years .

What do we know about the EU's affordable housing proposal?

The EU's executive branch unveiled the measures as part of an "affordable housing" package, which will allow local authorities to limit short-term rentals to address what European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera described as a "terrible crisis."

"When the market fails to deliver something as fundamental as an affordable home, public authorities have a responsibility to act," the Spanish politician said.

The measures seek to harmonize rules across the bloc, after attempts to crack down on Airbnb-style rentals by authorities in cities such as Paris, Berlin and Barcelona, among others, were met with legal challenges by rental and tourism companies.

The European Commission's Affordable Housing Act — which still needs to be approved by EU legislators and EU member states — would provide cities with legal support by clarifying when local authorities can act against housing companies without breaking EU single market rules.

Under the proposal, city and local authorities would be allowed to limit short-term and holiday rentals as well as curb the purchase of property for short-term letting in areas considered to be "under housing stress," the European Commission said.

For an area to be defined as "under stress," certain parameters — including the ratio between local housing prices and incomes — would have to be met.

Before restrictions can be introduced, cities would have to show that holiday rentals have had a major negative impact on the affordability or availability of housing for at least three years.

The proposed legislation will not impact landlords renting out their primary residence for short-term periods.

The Commission also recommended that authorities free up land for more housing and modernize planning and construction of new homes to address housing shortages.

How have rental companies reacted?

CCIA Europe, a lobbying group that represents Airbnb, among others, said the EU's measures fail to address the need for independent assessment of the restrictions.

"Europe will not solve its housing crisis by giving cities an EU framework to restrict short-term rentals and then letting them police their own ​compliance," CCIA's head of ⁠policy Alexandre Roure said in a statement.

"Without independent scrutiny or effective redress, this proposal will remain a paper tiger, leaving disproportionate restrictions ⁠in place and undermining ​the legal certainty the Affordable Housing Act is meant to provide," Roure added.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Syria: How the 'house of sisters' threat split society
entries.summary: Rumor has it that the 'house of sisters' is where kidnapped women from other Syrian sects are forced to convert to Islam. Nobody knows if it really exists, but it's being used to create communal tensions anyway.
entries.content:
Syria

Syria: How the 'house of sisters' threat split society

September 9, 2026

Rumor has it that the 'house of sisters' is where kidnapped women from other Syrian sects are forced to convert to Islam. Nobody knows if it really exists, but it's being used to create communal tensions anyway.

A knock on the door, a muted threat and then they made the decision to leave the country, says Layla, a math teacher and mother-of-three in her 40s.

Until recently, Layla — who didn't want DW to use her full name for security reasons — was living in Damascus, Syria's capital. She and her family are Alawites, the same religious sect as former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad, who are often targeted because they're seen as Assad's allies.

"But we never supported him, his father killed members of my family. We hated him actually," she told DW. Still, she describes feeling fearful when rebel groups entered Damascus in 2024 for the first time after the fall of the Assad regime, calling them "extremists."

At first, she and her husband decided to stay in Syria. But then a stranger came to the door.

"He told me 'we know your daughter plays piano and has dance lessons. You should stop that. If you don't, maybe we will take her to the house of the sisters," Layla recounts.

In conservative Islamic circles, women playing music and dancing for an audience is frowned upon. And Layla had heard about the so-called "house of the sisters" — she had read online it was a place where Syrian women from other sects were forced to convert to Islam. A few days later, the family decided to leave the country. They are now in Lebanon.

"I just don't want my children to grow up that way," Layla explains.

What is the 'house of sisters'?

Headlines about the "house of sisters" first really made waves in Syria in May after an Alawite university student Batoul Alloush, 21, was reported missing by her family, possibly kidnapped, only to turn up later wearing religious clothing and saying she left her family in order to convert to Islam.

There were already other stories of missing women, including from the Alawite minority. 

Reham Suleiman, a psychologist who works for the United Nations and with the Alawite community, told DW she has firsthand knowledge of several cases of kidnapping. "And it’s not just one incident or coincidence," she says. It is clear some of women were kidnapped for ransom money, revenge or forced marriage.

But other cases were apparently resolved when, for example, the women said they had been visiting friends, wanted to escape their families or had run away to a lover. Alloush herself said she wished to convert to Islam and leave her family. Her parents insist she's been drugged or coerced.

Organizations like Amnesty International and the UN's Commission of Inquiry on Syria say the cases — which number between 40 and 60 ­­— have not been fully investigated.

A political football

Syrian authorities did look into the "house of sisters." A spokesperson for Syria's Minister of Social Affairs, Hind Kabawat, told DW that the ministry has not licensed any facility with that name and that any unlicensed centers of this nature would be shut down.

Syrian fact-checking organizations like Verify-Sy found that pictures of the supposed "house of sisters" building were created with AI.

"A constant stream of unverified claims circulates on a daily basis concerning alleged kidnappings and killings, arrests and cases of torture in detention facilities," a spokesperson from Verify-Sy told DW.

"Verifying many of these is challenging when evidence available through open sources is scarce, contradictory or otherwise insufficient."

So whether the "house of sisters" exists in some form is unclear. But real or not, some groups appear to have instrumentalized it for their own agenda anyway, independent media outlet Shaam News Network, or SNN, wrote recently.

"Despite the absence of any physical evidence … social media platforms and pages began circulating 'the house' as an established fact," SNN wrote. "And it gradually became the focus of broader narratives about the 'organized kidnapping' of Alawite women."

International influencers

A private organization called the Syrian Investigation Mechanism, or SIM, founded in May 2026, links the "house of sisters" to a Muslim organization that proselytizes to gain new converts. SIM claimed the missing women were coerced into converting and held in "the house."

In an interview on YouTube, SIM director Yasser Shalati, who is based in Brandenburg, Germany, claims this is evidence of "demographic engineering." SIM did not reply to DW's requests for further comment.

A Berlin-based organization, the Union of Syrian Alawites in Europe, or USAE, has also repeatedly posted about the "house of sisters."

On his personal Facebook page, Muaiad Ibrahim, who is listed as USAE's deputy director in official court documents, regularly criticizes the new Syrian government and recently expressed support for Syria's highest religious scholar under the Assad regime, Ahmed Hassoun. In late August, Hassoun was sentenced to life in prison after being convicted of inciting civil war and complicity in intentional killing.

Other recently founded overseas organizations — including some that claim they have a network of millions of human rights advocates but link to incomplete websites — have also repeatedly disseminated stories about the "house of sisters."

Arab investigative journalism outfit DARAJ notes some of these organizations have been criticized for their apparent support of the Assad regime.  

The damage done?

"This kind of information ebbs and flows, but it does have a real impact and its quite powerful," says Gregory Waters, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, who's traveled extensively in Syria and monitors events on his site, Syria Revisited.

"It has the political intent to isolate Alawites, to make them fearful and keep them from engaging with the government, with [Syrian] Sunnis, and maybe to some extent, pull them towards insurgent [anti-government] networks."

Online propaganda feeds on real events within minority communities, adding to their existing fears, he says.

Verify Sy conducts a monthly audit of online disinformation, and researchers there say incitement is the second most common objective. Waters says Syrian authorities have been trying to rein in local influencers who spread disinformation, although obviously they can't impact those based overseas.

Like anywhere else in the world, you'll get a wide spectrum of opinions within every Syrian community, Waters notes. "There are there those who will insist that there's a program of ethnic cleansing, and there are others who say life is fine, we are fully integrated into the state."

Although it depends which part of the country you're looking at, he doesn't think relations between different communities are getting worse.

"In Syria, everything is unique to its local environment," Waters explains. "So in some places, we could say that walls between communities have hardened over the past two years and little progress has been made in reducing that. But even so, the walls are not getting higher."

Stabilization first

"Right now, generally speaking, the government in Damascus is busy establishing institutions, taking control of the security situation and trying to stabilize the country," argues Naseef Naeem, research director at the Berlin-based Candid Foundation, which consults on Syrian affairs. But sooner or later, Syria is going to need more of a national dialogue between different community groups, he says.

In the meantime, both he and Waters believe the Syrian economy, devastated after years of war, could hold the key to better relations.

"As soon as the economic recovery really gets underway, many of these phenomena will gradually disappear," Naeem told DW.

For example, Waters says, over summer, a lot of domestic tourists, many of them Sunni, made their way to the Syrian coast, an area where many Alawites live.

"There was a massive tourism boom," Waters explains. "Everybody's interacting and I've heard from friends there that there wasn't harassment, no violence. The government and security authorities really emphasized supporting the tourism industry in coastal areas this year and it's had a really positive impact."

Those kinds of inter-community contacts in real life "help reduce the impact of disinformation campaigns and the level of fear," he concludes.

Edited by: K. Hairsine

entries.title: LIV Golf in financial turmoil: what's next for the sport?
entries.summary: Six months after Saudi Arabia pulled funding from the breakaway organization, LIV Golf have filed for bankruptcy protection. Several of the world's best players signed on to LIV, so where does that leave golf?
entries.content:
September 9, 2026

Six months after Saudi Arabia pulled funding from the breakaway organization, LIV Golf have filed for bankruptcy protection. Several of the world's best players signed on to LIV, so where does that leave golf?

What has happened to LIV golf?

The breakaway golf tour, launched with much fanfare, billions of dollars of investment and a string of the world's best players, in 2021. But on Tuesday it filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States.

Bankruptcy protection is a way of keeping a company alive while it restructures its debts. In this case, LIV would be moving from being financed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), which pulled out in April, to being supported by BC Partners, a British investment firm.

"This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf," said the chief executive, Scott O'Neil.

According to documents related to the filing, LIV Golf has between $500m (€430 million) and $1 billion in estimated liabilities to at least 1,000 creditors. This includes an estimated $45 million to a group of top players like Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7 million), Jon Rahm ($7.5 million) and Dustin Johnson ($5.7million).

O'Neil added that LIV intends to move towards a "player-first ownership model," but detail is thin, and there is currently no schedule in place for 2027. Most of LIV's staff were laid off earlier this year.

What has caused LIV golf to go bankrupt?

The sudden withdrawal of the PIF, which had invested an estimated $5 billion in LIV Golf, is the over-riding reason. At the time, the PIF said that LIV Golf was "no longer consistent with the current phase of PIF's investment strategy."

This was considered evidence of the project's failure to overthrow the established PGA Tour or make much in the way of money or impact. While the huge prize money on offer lured away several big names, many more remained with the PGA Tour.

While Tuesday's legal move may buy LIV time, the withdrawal of Saudi funding, which was so key to its business model, gives O'Neil few options. To survive, it seems, it they must keep at least some of their big-name players while slimming down dramatically.

Is this further evidence of Saudi Arabia pulling out of sport?

It certainly seems that investment in golf is a thing of the past for the oil-rich, Gulf state. There have also been withdrawals of funding for tournaments, clubs or organizations in snooker, women's tennis, rugby and football. Saudi Arabia also backed away from its commitment to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games.

Sport was a key part of Vision 2030, a pet project of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that aimed to diversify the Saudi economy and, in the eyes of many, also help launder its reputation through sport and other cultural assets.

The uncertainty caused by conflict in the Middle East has meant even the vast wealth of the Saudi ruling class has taken a hit while projects like the resort of Trojena, set to be a key resort in those Winter Games, have been scaled back.

The same is true of Neom, a proposed World Cup venue for 2034. Planned as an entirely new type of city — 500 meters high (1,640 foot), built in a straight line and powered by renewable energy, Neom's construction has been significantly scaled back. The Guardian reported in late 2025 that several proposed World Cup stadium architects have been asked to rethink their plans to cut costs.

What will happen to the LIV golf players now?

It is unclear what will happen to the LIV golf players. The PGA Tour and LIV Golf have always had a frosty relationship. Any player leaving to join LIV was immediately suspended from the PGA Tour, which runs all of golf's major championships.

The 'returning member program', used by US golfer Brooks Koepka earlier this year to return to the PGA, briefly offered a potential pathway. It was designed as a "route back to elite performers who no longer have contractual limitations preventing them from complying with PGA Tour rules and regulations."

However it is was only open to players who left the PGA Tour at least two years ago and have won the Players Championship or one of the four majors.

DeChambeau, Cam Smith and Rahm were, therefore, the only players that qualified. But with that door now seemingly closed even to them, a return looks complex.

"I'm not part of the discussions but I'm pretty sure they aren't going to be welcomed back straight away," said Rory McIlroy, a six-time major winner who has been consistently critical of LIV, in August.

"They were offered this returning member program back in February, the one Brooks [Koepka] took, but that has come and gone, and I think it was said at the time that the deal they get going forward if they decide to come back would not be as good at the one Brooks got. So I'd say it will be a tough road back."

Edited by: Jonathan Harding
